title: The chronobiology textbook
lede: Twelve chapters on the rhythms of living things, from the molecular clock to migration, written by the students of one class.
description: The class's chronobiology textbook: twelve chapters on circadian, ultradian and infradian rhythms.

figure-1.alt: Flow diagram of GLP-1 signaling: food reaches the small intestine, which releases GLP-1; through the blood it triggers insulin secretion in the pancreas, and through the vagus nerve it signals fullness to the brain.

figure-1-2.alt: Venn diagram: melatonin and cortisol belong to the master clock, the food-entrainable oscillator and GLP-1 to peripheral clocks, and insulin, leptin and ghrelin to both.

figure-2.alt: Anatomical drawing of the body labeled with hunger signals: ghrelin made in the stomach, GLP-1 in the ileum, leptin in fat tissue, GLP-1 detected by the pancreas, and the brain responding to these hormones.

figure-4.alt: Diagram showing that while the liver processes ethanol, its usual metabolism of food and drink, mainly glucose, into ATP is blocked.

figure-5.alt: Diagram of aerobic respiration: glycolysis in the cytosol turns glucose into pyruvate, then pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain in the mitochondria produce most of the ATP, with NADH and FADH2 carrying electrons.

figure-6.alt: Reaction diagram: alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into acetaldehyde, then aldehyde dehydrogenase turns it into acetic acid, each step converting NAD+ to NADH.

figure-1.alt: Labeled cross-section of the human heart showing its four chambers, its valves, the aorta, the venae cavae and the pulmonary vessels.

figure-2.alt: Diagram of the heart's conduction system: the signal starts at the sinoatrial node, passes through the atrioventricular node and bundle of His, and spreads along the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers.

figure-2-2.alt: Diagram of the heart's nerve supply: parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve release acetylcholine to slow the heart, and sympathetic fibers from the spinal cord release norepinephrine to speed it up and strengthen each beat.

figure-4.alt: Diagram of a pacemaker: a pulse generator under the skin, with leads running through a vein into the right atrium and right ventricle.

figure-5.alt: Chest X-ray of an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator, labeled with the device, the high-voltage coils in the superior vena cava and right ventricle, and the pacing electrodes.

figure-6.alt: Illustration of a left ventricular assist device: a pump attached to the bottom of the heart's left ventricle, with a tube carrying blood to the aorta.

chapters.title: Neuronal activity: spikes and local field potentials
outline: Getting a signal from a recording

figure-11.alt: Leaky integrate-and-fire formula: tau m times d V over d t equals minus the quantity V of t minus V rest, plus R m times I of t.

figure-6.alt: Fourier transform formula: X of f equals the integral from minus infinity to infinity of x of t times e to the minus i 2 pi f t, d t.

figure-8.alt: Wavelet transform formula: W of a and b equals 1 over the square root of a, times the integral of x of t times the complex conjugate of psi of t minus b over a, d t.

figure-9.alt: Artificial neuron formula: y equals phi of the sum over i of w i times x i, plus b.

figure-a1.alt: Three stacked graphs over 120 milliseconds: an intracellular action potential rising from about minus 70 millivolts past threshold, extracellular spikes as brief sharp dips, and the local field potential as a slow, smooth wave.

figure-a2.alt: Five sine waves over one second showing the frequency bands: delta at 2 hertz, theta at 6, alpha at 10, beta at 20 and gamma at 40, each with more cycles.

figure-a3.alt: An LFP wave over 1.2 seconds with two neurons' spikes marked: neuron A fires near each peak and neuron B near each trough, at the same average rate.

figure-a4.alt: Three graphs over 2 seconds: a slow 2 hertz breathing cycle, the strength of a fast gamma rhythm rising and falling with it, and the combined signal showing fast oscillations in bursts on each cycle.

figure-a5.alt: Three panels of spike sorting: a raw recording with candidate spikes crossing a threshold, two different average spike shapes, and a scatter plot where spikes fall into two clusters, one per neuron.

figure-a6.alt: Three graphs: a raw signal of a slow rhythm with two brief 60 hertz bursts; its whole-recording power spectrum, with a tall peak at the slow frequency and a tiny one at 60 hertz; and a spectrogram that shows each burst at its time.

figure-a7.alt: Two graphs: a basic artificial neuron gives the same output value at every input step, while a spiking neuron fires brief pulses at specific times.
